hello.note: Ẹ is the respectful form for elders and strangers. Casual, to a friend: báwo ni?

goodbye.note: Also common: ó dìgbà (until next time).

please.note: Fuller form: ẹ jọ̀wọ́. To a friend or someone younger: jọ̀ọ́.

thank_you.note: To a friend or someone younger: o ṣé. Also ẹ ṣeun. Thank you very much: ẹ ṣé gan-an.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'it isn't worth thanks'. Also common: kò sí wàhálà (no trouble).

sorry.note: To a friend: má bínú. Ẹ pẹ̀lẹ́ shows sympathy (someone tripped or is unwell); it is not an apology.

excuse_me.note: Same word as 'please'; the drawn-out o calls attention. Often followed by sà (sir) or mà (ma'am).

good_morning.note: To a friend or someone younger: káàárọ̀. The reply is the same greeting.

how_are_you.note: Casual, to a friend: báwo ni? Also common: ṣé àlàáfíà ni?

im_fine.note: Very common reply: a dúpẹ́ (we give thanks).

whats_your_name.note: In speech often kí lorúkọ yín? To a child or friend: kí ni orúkọ rẹ?

nice_to_meet_you.text: Inú mi dùn láti pàdé yín
nice_to_meet_you.note: To a friend or someone younger: … láti pàdé rẹ.

where_from.note: To a friend or someone younger: ibo lo ti wá?

im_from.note: Also natural, stressing the place: … ni mo ti wá.

speak_english.note: Also common: ṣé ẹ gbọ́ Gẹ̀ẹ́sì? (do you understand English?)

speak_slowly.note: Please say it again: ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ tún un sọ.

where.note: Also ibo? Where is …?: ibo ni … wà?

what.note: Pardon, what did you say?: kí lẹ sọ?

why.note: Also means 'what's wrong?'. More formal: nítorí kí ni?

how_much.note: In quick market speech: èló lèyí? Bargaining is normal.

where_bathroom.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ibo ni ilé ìgbọ̀nsẹ̀ wà?
where_bathroom.note: Many people simply use the English word toilet. Balùwẹ̀ is a room for bathing.

can_you_help.text: Ṣé ẹ lè ràn mí lọ́wọ́?

what_time.note: Answer, e.g.: aago mẹ́ta ló lù (it's three o'clock).

one.note: After a noun: kan (ìwé kan, one book).

two.note: After a noun: méjì (ìwé méjì, two books).

three.note: After a noun: mẹ́ta (ìwé mẹ́ta, three books).

four.note: After a noun: mẹ́rin (ìwé mẹ́rin, four books).

five.note: After a noun: márùn-ún (ìwé márùn-ún, five books).

six.note: After a noun: mẹ́fà (ìwé mẹ́fà, six books).

seven.note: After a noun: méje (ìwé méje, seven books).

eight.note: After a noun: mẹ́jọ (ìwé mẹ́jọ, eight books).

nine.note: After a noun: mẹ́sàn-án (ìwé mẹ́sàn-án, nine books).

ten.note: After a noun: mẹ́wàá (ìwé mẹ́wàá, ten books).

tea.note: In Nigeria tíì can mean any hot drink, including cocoa drinks.

im_hungry.note: Literally 'hunger is killing me'. I'm thirsty: òùngbẹ ń gbẹ mí.

menu_please.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ fún mi ní mẹ́nù
menu_please.note: A local bùkà rarely has a menu; ask kí lẹ ní? (what do you have?)

bill_please.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, èló ni gbogbo rẹ̀?
bill_please.note: Literally 'how much is it all?', the usual way to ask for the bill.

delicious.note: Very tasty: ó dùn gan-an! Dùn also means sweet or pleasant.

no_meat.note: Fish (ẹja) is often not counted as meat; add mi kì í jẹ ẹja if needed.

enjoy_meal.note: To a friend: gbádùn oúnjẹ rẹ! People eating often invite you: ẹ wá jẹun (come and eat).

left.note: Turn left: ẹ yà sí òsì.

right.note: Turn right: ẹ yà sí ọ̀tún.

straight_ahead.note: Go straight on: ẹ máa lọ tààrà.

airport.note: In everyday speech the English word airport is also common.

train_station.note: The train itself: ọkọ̀ ojú irin.

want_to_go.note: Sí merges with a following vowel: lọ sí ilé → lọ sílé (go home).

is_it_far.note: Replies: ó jìnnà (it's far), kò jìnnà (it's not far).

too_expensive.note: Bargaining is expected: ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ dín in kù (please bring the price down).

cheaper.text: Ṣé ẹ ní èyí tí kò wọ́n tó báyìí?

id_like_this.note: Also natural: èyí ni mo fẹ́ (this is the one I want).

pay_card.text: Ṣé mo lè fi káàdì sanwó?
pay_card.note: In Nigeria people often ask: ṣé ẹ ní POS? (do you have a card machine?)

cash.note: Many people simply say the English word cash. Bank transfers are also very common.

open.note: Shop signs in Nigeria are nearly always in English.

closed.note: We've closed for the day: a ti tì. Shop signs are nearly always in English.

big.note: After a noun: ilé ńlá (a big house). It's big: ó tóbi.

small.note: After a noun: ilé kékeré (a small house). It's small: ó kéré.

today.note: Inside a sentence: lónìí, e.g. mo máa lọ lónìí (I'll go today).

later.note: Often shortened to tó bá yá.

good_evening.note: To a friend: káalẹ́. In the afternoon: ẹ káàsán.

good_night.note: Also: ẹ sùn re o (sleep well).

wait_moment.note: Dúró means wait, stop and stand.

need_doctor.note: Also common: mo fẹ́ rí dókítà (I want to see a doctor).

im_lost.note: Also: ọ̀nà ti dà mí rú (I've got mixed up about the way).

dont_feel_well.note: Careful form: ara mi kò yá.

pharmacy.note: In everyday speech most people say chemist, borrowed from English.

lost_phone.text: Mo ti sọ fóònù mi nù
lost_phone.note: If it was stolen: wọ́n ti jí fóònù mi.

allergic.note: People also use the English word allergy.

i_like_it.note: Of something you see and fancy: ó wù mí.

dont_like_it.note: Of something you see: kò wù mí.

welcome.note: To a friend or someone younger: káàbọ̀.

my_family.note: Also: ìdílé mi (my household). Mi follows the noun: ìyá mi (my mother).

mother.note: Also màmá. Ìyá is also a respectful way to address an older woman.

father.note: Also a respectful way to address an older man.

brother.note: Siblings are usually named by age: ẹ̀gbọ́n (older), àbúrò (younger), e.g. ẹ̀gbọ́n mi ọkùnrin.

sister.note: Everyday: ẹ̀gbọ́n mi obìnrin (my older sister), àbúrò mi obìnrin (my younger sister).

child.note: My child: ọmọ mi. Son: ọmọkùnrin; daughter: ọmọbìnrin.

friend.note: Same word for a man or a woman. Close friend: ọ̀rẹ́ tímọ́tímọ́.

this_is_my_friend.note: Same for a male or female friend. Also: èyí ni ọ̀rẹ́ mi.

are_you_married.note: Also, to a man: ṣé ẹ ti níyàwó? (have you a wife?) To a woman: ṣé ẹ ti lọ́kọ? (have you a husband?)

have_children.note: Bímọ (have a child) is said of men and women alike. Also: ṣé ẹ lọ́mọ?

monday.note: On Monday: lọ́jọ́ Ajé. English day names are also common in everyday speech.

wednesday.note: Written as one word. On Wednesday: lọ́jọ́rú.

thursday.note: Written as one word. On Thursday: lọ́jọ́bọ̀.

friday.note: Also common, especially among Muslims: Ọjọ́ Jímọ̀.

sunday.note: Also very common: Ọjọ́ Ìsinmi (day of rest).

weekend.note: Also: ìparí ọ̀sẹ̀. Many people simply say weekend, from English.

what_day.note: In speech often ọjọ́ wo lòní? Answer, e.g.: Ọjọ́ Ajé lòní (today is Monday).

next_week.note: Inside a sentence: lọ́sẹ̀ tó ń bọ̀. Last week: ọ̀sẹ̀ tó kọjá.

eleven.note: After a noun: mọ́kànlá (ìwé mọ́kànlá, eleven books).

twelve.note: After a noun: méjìlá (ìwé méjìlá, twelve books).

fifteen.note: Literally five short of twenty. After a noun: mẹ́ẹ̀ẹ́dógún (ìwé mẹ́ẹ̀ẹ́dógún, fifteen books).

twenty.note: Twenty years: ogún ọdún. Yoruba counts in twenties: forty is ogójì (two twenties).

thirty.note: Twenty-five is ẹ̀ẹ́dọ́gbọ̀n, literally five short of thirty.

hundred.note: Literally five twenties. A hundred naira: ọgọ́rùn-ún náírà.

thousand.note: A thousand naira: ẹgbẹ̀rún náírà. Two thousand: ẹgbàá.

how_old.note: To a friend or child: ọmọ ọdún mélòó lo jẹ́? Asking an elder's age directly can seem rude.

years_old.note: E.g. ọmọ ọdún méjìlá ni mí (I'm 12). From twenty, round numbers go first: ọmọ ogún ọdún ni mí (I'm 20).

red.note: It's red: ó pupa. Traditionally pupa also covers orange and pink shades.

blue.note: The indigo of traditional dyed cloth. Many people simply say blue, from English.

green.note: Literally 'leaf colour'. Many people simply say green, from English.

yellow.note: Named after the yellow hog-plum fruit; also òféfèé. Many people simply say yellow, from English.

black.note: It's black: ó dúdú. Also used for any dark colour.

what_colour.note: Also common: àwọ̀ wo ló jẹ́?

this_one.note: Also common: eléyìí. I want this one: mo fẹ́ èyí.

that_one.note: I want that one: mo fẹ́ ìyẹn.

another_one.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ fún mi ní ọ̀kan sí i
another_one.note: Sí i means 'more'. A different one: òmíràn.

its_hot.note: Very hot: ooru mú gan-an. I'm hot: ooru ń mú mi.

its_cold.note: I'm cold: òtútù ń mú mi.

its_raining.note: It's about to rain: òjò fẹ́ rọ̀.

its_sunny.note: Careful with tones: oòrùn is sun, oorun is sleep.

its_windy.note: Very windy: afẹ́fẹ́ ń fẹ́ gan-an. A storm: ìjì.

weather_today.text: Báwo ni ojú ọjọ́ ṣe rí lónìí?
weather_today.note: Ojú ọjọ́ (weather) is literally 'the face of the day'.

summer.note: The hot dry season. Nigeria's other season is the rainy season, ìgbà òjò.

winter.note: Literally 'cold season'. The cool, dusty harmattan in Nigeria is ọyẹ́.

have_reservation.text: Mo ti gba yàrá síbí tẹ́lẹ̀
have_reservation.note: Literally 'I already took a room here'. Hotel staff usually use the English word booking.

room.note: Also any room in a house. Bedroom: yàrá ìbùsùn.

passport.note: Literally 'travel document'. Most people simply say passport, from English.

luggage.note: Also means any load or goods. My luggage: ẹrù mi.

wifi_password.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, kí ni pásíwọ̀ọ̀dù Wi-Fi yín?
wifi_password.note: Both words come from English and are said much as in English.

check_out_time.text: Aago mélòó ni mo gbọ́dọ̀ fi yàrá sílẹ̀?
check_out_time.note: Literally 'what time must I leave the room?' Staff often use the English check-out.

map.note: Literally 'picture of the land'. Many people simply say map, from English.

bus.note: In Lagos the yellow minibuses are called dáńfó.

next_train.text: Ìgbà wo ni ọkọ̀ ojú irin tó kàn máa gbéra?
next_train.note: Tó kàn means 'the next one'; gbéra means 'set off'.

is_this_seat_free.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ṣé ẹnìkan ti gba àyè yìí?
is_this_seat_free.note: Literally 'has someone taken this place?' Can I sit here?: ṣé mo lè jókòó síbí?

what_do_you_do.note: To a friend or someone younger: iṣẹ́ wo lò ń ṣe?

i_work_in.note: E.g. mo ń ṣiṣẹ́ ní ilé ìwòsàn (I work at a hospital).

im_student.note: Same for a man or a woman.

office.note: Workplace in general: ibi iṣẹ́. I'm going to work: mo ń lọ síbi iṣẹ́.

meeting.note: I have a meeting: mo ní ìpàdé. Pàdé means 'to meet'.

im_busy.note: Literally 'my hands are occupied'. Very busy: ọwọ́ mi dí gan-an.

day_off.note: Literally 'day of rest'. I'm off today: mi ò ṣiṣẹ́ lónìí.

colleague.note: Same for a man or a woman. Literally 'one I work together with'.

lets_start.note: To one friend: jẹ́ ká bẹ̀rẹ̀.

good_job.note: To a friend or someone younger: o ṣe dáadáa! Also common: ẹ káre o!

table_for_two.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, a fẹ́ tábìlì fún ènìyàn méjì
table_for_two.note: At a local bùkà you simply sit wherever there is space.

what_recommend.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, kí ló dára jù níbí?
what_recommend.note: Literally 'what's best here?'. Also: kí lẹ rò pé kí n jẹ? (what do you think I should eat?)

not_spicy.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ má fi ata sí i
not_spicy.note: Ó ta means 'it's spicy'. Just a little pepper: ata díẹ̀.

vegetarian_food.note: Literally 'food without meat'. Soups often contain fish (ẹja) or crayfish (edé).

more_water.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ fún mi ní omi sí i

no_sugar.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ má fi ṣúgà sí i
no_sugar.note: Just a little sugar: ṣúgà díẹ̀.

im_full.note: Very full: mo ti yó bámúbámú.

takeaway.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ dì í kí n mú un lọ
takeaway.note: Literally 'wrap it so I can take it away'.

it_was_delicious.note: No past tense needed: the same sentence also means 'the food is delicious'.

keep_change.note: Literally 'leave the change'. Many Nigerians call change balance.

head.note: In Yoruba thought orí also means one's destiny.

stomach.note: For aches Yoruba uses inú (inside): inú ń run mí (I have a stomach ache).

have_fever.note: Ibà also means malaria, the usual suspect in Nigeria.

medicine.note: Also covers traditional herbal remedies. To take medicine: lo oògùn.

call_ambulance.note: Literally 'vehicle for the sick'. Many people simply say ambulance.

dentist.note: Literally 'tooth doctor'. Toothache: eyín ń dùn mí.

need_rest.note: Also: mo fẹ́ sinmi díẹ̀ (I'd like to rest a bit).

feel_better.note: Fully recovered: ara mi ti yá.

get_well.note: Often after ẹ pẹ̀lẹ́ o (sorry you're unwell). The reply: àmín.

lets_meet.note: To one friend: jẹ́ ká pàdé. Where shall we meet?: ibo la ti máa pàdé?

are_you_free.note: Literally 'will you find time tomorrow?' To a friend: ṣé o máa ráyè lọ́la?

call_me.note: To a friend: pè mí. To make clear it's a phone call: ẹ pè mí lórí fóònù.

your_number.note: To a friend: kí ni nọ́ńbà fóònù rẹ? Numbers are usually read out in English.

have_nice_day.text: Ọjọ́ òní á dára fún yín o!
have_nice_day.note: Wishes are often said as blessings. The reply: àmín (amen) or àṣẹ.

good_luck.note: Literally 'it will be good'. Also: Ọlọ́run á ṣe é o! (God will see it through)

happy_birthday.note: To a friend: o kú ọjọ́ ìbí! Many people simply say happy birthday in English.

thanks_a_lot.note: To a friend or someone younger: o ṣé gan-an. Also: ẹ ṣeun púpọ̀.

miss_you.note: To an elder or several people: àárò yín ń sọ mí.
